title: UN gives Bangladesh three more years before leaving LDC status
excerpt: Graduation moves to 24 November 2029. Economists say the extra time only helps if trade, revenue and banking reforms speed up.
content:
The UN General Assembly has extended Bangladesh’s preparation period for leaving the least developed country (LDC) group by three years. Graduation moves from 24 November 2026 to 24 November 2029.

The Assembly adopted the decision on 29 October at its 81st session, The Business Standard reported. Uruguay tabled the proposal on Bangladesh’s behalf. Nepal received the same three-year extension.

The resolution grants the extra time “on an exceptional basis”. It urges Bangladesh to press ahead with reforms and its smooth transition strategy, with international support, and to report progress every year to the UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP).

How the decision came about

  • Bangladesh met all three graduation criteria (income per person, human assets and economic and environmental vulnerability) in UN reviews in 2018 and 2021.
  • The General Assembly approved graduation in November 2021. Because of Covid-19, Bangladesh was given five years to prepare instead of the usual three.
  • On 18 February 2026 the government asked the CDP for more time, citing global economic uncertainty, changes in trade, energy and supply chain risks and domestic economic problems.
  • The CDP backed the request, and the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) sent it to the General Assembly on 21 July 2026.

What business leaders and economists said

Mahmud Hasan Khan, president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), called it good news for exporters. He said the time should be used to improve infrastructure and logistics and to pursue trade agreements, according to the newspaper.

Fahmida Khatun, distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said more time alone would not make the economy more competitive. She called for reforms in trade, revenue collection, banking and infrastructure, and for a reform plan with deadlines and progress reports every six months.

Mustafa Abid Khan, chief executive of the Bangladesh Foreign Trade Institute, said the extension mattered most for intellectual property rules and trade talks, but warned that benefits would be lost if business continued as usual.

Why it matters

LDC status brings duty-free access to markets such as the EU, UK, Canada and Japan, flexible patent rules for medicines and some concessional finance. A 2025 UNCTAD analysis cited by The Business Standard estimated exports could fall by about 32% if those preferences were lost. Garments and pharmaceuticals are most exposed. For NGOs and development partners, the extra three years also delay changes to LDC-specific aid and loan terms, at a time when aid is already shrinking, as a recent Atlantic Council brief showed.

The World Bank’s October Development Update pointed to weak banks, energy shortages and low revenue as the main brakes on growth. Those are the same reforms economists now say the extra time must be used for.

What to watch

Whether the government publishes a time-bound transition plan, its first annual progress report to the CDP, and talks with the EU and UK on trade terms after 2029.
